entities.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the residual radiation from the Big Bang, which marked the beginning of the universe around 13.8 billion years ago. This phenomenon was first observed in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who discovered the signal while conducting radio astronomy experiments at Bell Labs in New Jersey, USA. The CMB is a key tool for understanding the universe's origins, evolution, and composition, and its study has led to numerous breakthroughs in our understanding of cosmology, particle physics, and the nature of space and time. The CMB's discovery has also had significant implications for the fields of astrophysics, cosmology, and the search for dark matter and dark energy, which are thought to play a crucial role in the universe's accelerating expansion. The CMB's legacy can be seen in the many experiments and missions that have been dedicated to studying it, including the COBE, WMAP, and Planck satellites, as well as the upcoming CMB-S4 experiment. The CMB's impact on our understanding of the universe is a testament to the power of human curiosity and the importance of scientific inquiry in advancing our knowledge of the cosmos.
